title: Quality, clean code, flexibility, speed, and communication
metaTitle: How a design studio’s standards show up
excerpt: Quality, clean code, flexibility, speed, and communication are behaviors you can see on a project. Each one shows up in the work, the repository, or the way a change is handled.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table. The table is a working review, where standards are visible in the work itself.
caption: Standards show up in the review, not on a poster. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What does quality look like during a project?
faqs.answer: Quality is a page a stranger can read, with contrast that holds, focus that shows, and words that say what the company does. It includes the empty and error states, not only the hero. You can point at it in a review. You should not have to take it on faith from a slogan.

faqs.question: What does clean code mean for a founder?
faqs.answer: Clean code means a later editor can find the headline, the sections, and the images without a treasure hunt. The repository is yours, in a stack a competent developer can read. Cleverness that only the original author can touch is not the standard.

faqs.question: How should flexibility and speed coexist?
faqs.answer: Flexibility means the process can change when the offer changes, with the date adjusted in writing. Speed means the public page stays fast while that happens. A change that makes the page heavy should be discussed against Core Web Vitals, not absorbed silently and discovered after launch.

markdown:
How a design studio works is visible in behavior, not in a slogan. On a Hanabi project the five differences are quality, clean code, flexibility, speed, and communication. Each one is something you can see while the work is happening.

The studio’s own line is the same list in plainer words: clarity over complexity, quality, clean code, a process that can change, speed, and plain communication. What follows is what those words mean on a Tuesday, in a file, in a review.

## Quality you can point at

Quality is the page doing its job for a stranger. The offer is understandable. The type is readable. The action is obvious. The brand feels like one idea from the first screen into the interface.

You can check pieces of that without a design degree. The W3C’s [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) group the basics into four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. In a review, that becomes concrete. Text has enough contrast. A keyboard user can see focus. Buttons have names. The page still makes sense if images are slow. Hanabi does not treat this as a certificate you buy at the end. It is part of done.

Quality also means the screens teams skip. An empty state that tells you what to do. An error that says what to fix. A confirmation that repeats the promise checkout just made. A hero with no failure state is a poster. The product is the set of states.

You should see this in the work in progress, not only at launch. If a review never looks at mobile, at focus, or at the unhappy path, the quality bar is still a sentence on a site. Ask to see those. A studio that holds the bar will be glad you asked.

## Clean code as a file you can find

Clean code, on a marketing site or a product interface, means the next person can find the headline, the sections, and the images. The repository is structured. The components match the brand instead of fighting it. Types in TypeScript catch a broken prop before a stranger does.

You do not have to read the code to test the claim. Ask where the homepage headline lives. Ask what you would edit to change a price, a project name, or a nav label. If the answer is a treasure hunt through a page builder, the code is not clean for the team that has to live with it. If the answer is a field or a clearly named file, the standard is real.

Ownership is part of cleanliness. The repo, the domain, and the content logins should be yours. Hanabi builds with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, and deploys in the way a later developer can follow. Design lives in Figma, beside the code, not instead of it. A build you cannot open is not a clean build. It is a rental.

Clean does not mean elaborate. A small set of components you actually use is cleaner than a kit of variants nobody asked for. The same idea governs a small brand system: one type pair, a short color list, and files people can find. The client portal exists so those files, the docs, and the project updates do not end in a chat scroll.

## Flexibility when the offer shifts

Flexibility is a process that can change. The offer will move. A sentence will be wrong once you see it on the page. A product you meant to feature will be out of stock. A page you thought you needed will turn out to be vanity.

The behavior is a written trade. The new thing enters the scope, and something else leaves, or the date moves. You can see it in the channel: a decision, an owner, a revised edge. What you should not see is silent absorption, where every new idea is accepted and the date stays fictional.

Flexibility is also a refusal. A studio that will change anything, including the part that makes the page clear, is not being flexible. It is being unguided. Hanabi’s version is clarity over complexity. If a requested addition makes the first screen harder to understand, the studio should say so and show the alternative. You can still choose the addition. The choice will be visible.

This is why early slices matter. A loose idea gets a first slice, not a fake map of the whole product. When the slice teaches you something, the process bends. The bend is the flexibility. The record of the bend is how you know it happened.

## Speed with a number

Speed is a behavior on the public page. It is not a claim that the studio works weekends.

Google’s [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) are the numbers worth using, because they describe what a person feels. Largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds. Interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds. Cumulative layout shift under 0.1. In practice that means the main image is not enormous, the page does not jump when it loads, and a tap gets a response.

You can see the standard when a request threatens it. A full-screen background video, a stack of chat widgets, a font that loads three families. The flexible response is not an automatic yes. It is a check: we can do this if the page still meets the bar, or we can do a lighter version that keeps the idea. Hanabi’s marketing work is held to that bar on purpose: static where it can be, motion that respects reduced motion, images served in a way that does not block the first view.

Speed of communication is a different word, and it belongs in the next section. Do not let “we move fast” replace a page that loads slowly. The page is the one your customer meets.

## Communication you can audit

Communication is clear updates, honest timelines, and fewer surprises. You can audit it without a survey.

There is one channel. Decisions that change scope or date are written down. A weekly note says what moved, what is blocked, and whether the date holds. When something slips, you hear it while there is still time to choose.

The tone is plain. You are not managed with urgency, and you are not left to infer status from a quiet Figma file. If the studio needs the offer sentence, the photos, or access, the ask is specific. If you need a day to think, the timeline says what that day costs.

You should also hear disagreement. A partner who only agrees is storing the surprise for launch week. Plain communication includes “this will make the page worse, here is why, here is the other option.” That sentence is the quality bar and the communication bar in the same moment.

The habits that keep those updates from going soft are their own topic. Read [communication habits that keep a build on track](/blog/communication-that-keeps-a-build-on-track) when you want the channel, the written decision, and the cadence spelled out as a practice.

If you want to see whether this is how a project with Hanabi would actually feel, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring a real constraint. The call should sound like the standards above: specific, owned, and short.
